en: Oṃ.

(Then enters Mālyavān, seated and deep in thought. Mālyavān: My friend, from the moment I first heard the news concerning the entire event at Siddhāśrama, ever since then—[I have been troubled by him] who, from afar, brushed aside the son of Tāṭakā—who resembles a mountain—as if he were a mere blade of grass.
Alas! That prince, the slayer of Subāhu and the foe of Tāṭakā, torments my heart.

What wonder is there that he slew his numerous followers in a single moment? For Rāma split in two the bow of Śambhu—which the Lotus-born Brahmā had fashioned through the excellence of the prowess of the nectar-eating gods—and he, the immeasurable one, received from Viśvāmitra, the disciple of the sage Kṛśāśva, the divine secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of weapons that brings about victory. //2//
While our messenger looked on, the mature sage forcibly performed at that time a marvel by bestowing divine weapons upon the two Rāvaṇas. //3//
For:
"The humiliation of that king by the capture of Sītā as a prisoner has been repelled; the gods' exclusive devotion toward us has been rendered lax.
Indeed, from the sound of the *nāndī* onwards, they performed auspicious rites at that time, yet almost all of them now undergo a transformation as his majesty is shattered. (4)
How did our dear Śūrpaṇakhā arrive?
(Entering Śūrpaṇakhā: Victory, victory to my maternal grandfather!
Mālyavān: Child, sit down. What conversation can there be in the presence of the king?
Śūrpaṇakhā: It is said that the wedding ceremonies were concluded there. Furthermore, the great sage Agastya has sent the excellent bow of Mahendra, which serves as an auspicious gift for Rāma.
Mālyavān: Those weapons of inconceivable power that exist in the worlds are transmitted by the Brahman-sages to Rāma.
(Reflecting:
The weapon of the Kshatriya is unfailing when it is an act of grace toward Brahmins;
and that Kshatriya energy, when united with the power of Brahman, is difficult to withstand. (5)
Śūrpaṇakhā: Even if he were merely a human being, what cause for concern would there be in this?
Mālyavān: Child, do not speak thus!
For from his very birth, Rāghava was a certain wonder in this world; what need is there to mention his mortality, when his deeds are sung even by gods and asuras?
Sages and gods bestow power upon objects through their superior reasoning; yet at the time of granting the boon, Brahmā did not speak of fear arising from a mortal. (6)
Moreover:
By his very nature he is the protector of Dharma, while we are the enemies of Dharma; thus, an inevitable conflict has arisen between us and our powerful rival. (7)

Śūrpaṇakhā: There is no doubt. Just as the ten-faced one stands with his face bowed, his rolling eyes being drawn away by the twenty side-glances of those with slightly bent brows, I know that this cruel affliction of heart-pain will not cease in this manner.
Mālyavān: Oh, how truly remarkable!
The seven self-born progenitors of the world, the teachers at the beginning of the ages, are indeed worthy of worship; yet, are we and they not dear as kinsmen to the King of Videha?
How then has this sense of deficiency arisen in the heart of the Lord of the World, the descendant of Pulastya, who blazes with splendor and whose ascetic power is so difficult to approach? (8)
Or rather:

Even though his desire has been made manifest, the Lord does not obtain the fruit; on the contrary, the son of Daśaratha, acting with hostility and contrary conduct, is joined with that maiden. How can the proud ten-faced Lord of the World endure the excellence of another, the ruin of his own honor and fame, and [the loss of] this jewel among women? (9)
(An attendant enters halfway from behind the scenes. This palm-leaf, upon which characters have been inscribed with *tāla* resin, has been brought by that messenger whom you sent to Paraśurāma.
(Having introduced [the matter], he exits. Mālyavān: (Taking it, he reads:)
RĪṂ Svasti! From Mahendradvīpa, Paraśurāma sends his respectful greetings to the minister Mālyavān in Laṅkā.
RĪṂ.
Śūrpaṇakhā: How is it that my lord draws with such ill-executed strokes?

Mālyavān: Right here, having congratulated the Lord of Laṅkā, who is a supreme devotee of Maheśvara, he says: "It is known to you that we have granted a pledge of safety to the ascetics dwelling at the holy sites of the Daṇḍaka forest. It has been heard that certain individuals there, such as Virādha, Danu, Kabandha, and others, are practicing sorcery against them. Therefore, please restrain them and follow our virtuous conduct and our Maheśvara-inspired affection for their welfare. Avoiding transgression against Brāhmaṇas will lead to your own prosperity;
furthermore, Paraśurāma, the son of Jamadagni, is your friend and would be displeased otherwise. (10)
Thus [it is said].
Śūrpaṇakhā: This introduction is somewhat slow, steady, and profound in its delivery.
Mālyavān: Oh, what is this being said? This is indeed the son of Jamadagni!
Having accumulated tranquility through his own excellence in lineage, asceticism, learning, prowess, and action, he remains free from worldly desire due to his total renunciation.
Out of some casual affection for Śiva, he identifies himself with us; yet, like a sovereign, he becomes exceedingly stern whenever a task must be performed. (11)
(Thus she thinks. Śūrpaṇakhā: What are you thinking?
Mālyavān:

Child, if the destroyer of Śambhu’s bow should advance against his disciple and he cannot endure it—if, through the intensity of their mutual fury, there should be a clash between the two in battle—then that indeed would be pleasing to us. (12)

Even if victory were achieved by either side, if the slayer of Kṣatriyas should defeat the prince, that wrathful man would not desist until he had struck him down; and thus our desired goal—the death of Rāma—would be accomplished. But an Ikṣvāku king, being victorious and devoted to the Brahmins, would never strike a Brahmin Ṛṣi. Even when one’s own welfare is at stake, he would not employ a weapon against one who has withdrawn from combat; and thus, [our purpose] would be difficult to achieve.
Śūrpaṇakhā: What is the difference?

Mālyavān: If the son of Jamadagni, observing his vow as a forest-dweller, were to slay the descendant of Raghu, even after killing him he would remain just as he was before. However, the prince must be restrained while he is intent on rising again. If one were to overcome that very person—who is currently possessed of the excellence of energy and power and who conquers through righteousness—then everyone would acknowledge him as the victor. At that very moment, the gods, who have been forcibly suppressed and are perpetually incensed, would violently seize this man and empower him;
for the provocation of the subjects against those who have conquered the Asuras is a constant consequence of their insults.

Even toward that Kārtavīrya, whose conduct was fierce in his destruction of the descendants of Pulastya and whom the sage Paraśurāma had previously confined within a circle [of arrows] as a means to conclude the history of all the kṣatriyas—toward him too, Rāma, the lord of the universe, who conducts himself with the gentleness of dharma despite possessing full capability, has brought about a fitting subjugation by casting off all improper treatment. //13//
Śūrpaṇakhā: Then what was thought about here now?
Mālyavān: "The incitement of Paraśurāma must be carried out."
Śūrpaṇakhā: On the other hand, there is great fault.

Mālyavān: Even in that case, it will be countered according to our power. However, if those very elements are the same and those very powers are the same, then we cannot conceive of the defeat of Paraśurāma. (14)

Therefore, arise! Let us go to Mahendra Island itself to rouse the son of Jamadagni for our departure toward Mithilā; for the venerable descendant of Bhṛgu resides there. Deep due to his majesty, foremost in purity, and exceedingly virtuous, he is like a mass of merit—serene and bestowing happiness upon all.
Through the excellence of his sovereignty and the purity resulting from his austerities, he strengthens the quality of goodness (*sattva*) and drives away evil. (15)
(Thus they both exit. //The Interlude//
(Offstage: O you who dwell in the noble families of the city of Videha! May you inform Rāmabhadra, who has entered the maidens' inner apartments:

"Even Kārtavīrya—whose arms were perfected in the strength to uproot Kailāsa and the prowess to conquer the three worlds, and who was difficult to subdue as he humbled the pride of battle even against the descendant of Pulastya—is [now surpassed by him]."
By whose wrath, in former times, he became like a tree whose massive trunk-bonds were split by axes and whose thick branch-stems were severed at their joints, leaving only the roots. //16//

This very hero, the son of Jamadagni—who has executed the total destruction of the Kṣatriya order twenty-one times without fail; who, by splitting Mount Krauñca, brought about the unprecedented descent of the swans upon the surface of the earth;

and who is the conqueror of Tāraka, the wielder of the discus against the hosts of Gaṇas led by Heramba and Bhṛṅgin—approaches you, O Arjuna, questioning you out of anger at the breaking of his guru’s bow by Hari. (17)
(Then enters Rāma, along with Sītā and her friends, filled with both composure and agitation.

Rāma: By good fortune, the Lord of the Bhṛgus—the great treasure-house of noble qualities, whose every deed has been purified by the ancient tradition of the divine Lord who burnt the city of Tripura—has arrived as my disciple.
He desires to see me; yet, casting aside all shame, this innocent girl, through her agitation and fear, reveals to me a love for me that is unrestrained by her noble birth. (18)
Sītā: Friend Saḥodā, how is this so now?
Friends, Prince, enough of this haste!
Rāma: Enthusiasm does not deserve such distaste for the defense of the city.
Friends, it is heard that this Paraśurāma—who has repeatedly liberated the entire world from oppression and whose fierce resolve and daring have become manifest—is on his way.

Rāma: Why do you summarize the majesty of this great treasury of supreme knowledge with only a single part? He is the one who—having thrice seven times cleared the quarters of the dense thickets of uprooted royal lineages by the strength of his arm, which is praiseworthy for its celebrated victory over Kārttikeya;

and having then given the earth, together with its islands, to his preceptor Kaśyapa at the Aśvamedha sacrifice; now stands performing penance on the bank of the Viṣayā, where the ocean has been diverted by his weapons. (19)
(Offstage:

Alas! The sage Bhārgava, intent on searching for Rāma, enters the very inner apartments of the princesses in a rage—his progress unimpeded by the doorkeepers, whose eyes are somehow terrified and whose faces are cast down as their gaze is struck by his sight; while those attendants, despondent at the loss of their composure, raise cries of "Alas! in every direction. (20)
Rāma: Surely these very ones are the authors of the manual on the rules of conduct for students. So how can this learned man be so negligent? Very well, I shall approach him.
(He walks about with firm and majestic strides.

Friends! Alas, the entire inner apartment is filled with the lamentations of a distressed and agitated retinue, crying out everywhere, "O Lord Moon-faced Rāmacandra! O Son-in-law! Therefore, Princess, you yourself must entreat the young prince.
Sītā: Therefore, let us go quickly and comfort our noble husband, who is distressed by the wind.
(Thus she walks about.
Friends! O Prince, look at the princess, her gait faltering and stumbling as she struggles to break free from her haste.
Rāma:
(Turning back with affectionate compassion) Surely, O timid one, you must be comforted by these noble ladies themselves.

Friends! Friend, friend! You always describe before us with overflowing affection this lotus-face of his—which is capable of churning the triple world of gods and asuras, which is the auspicious mark of the prosperity of the lofty Jālandhara dynasty, and which possesses the beauty of a full-blown blue lotus—yet why are you trembling when the prince is facing Vijayā?
Sītā: He is Paraśurāma, the one who caused distress to all the Kṣatriyas.
Rāma: My beloved, compose yourself and turn back.
Let this trembling caused by the agitation of fear, fatigue, and rashness be endured for a moment by your limbs, which possess the luster of lovely Madhūka flowers and are the very essence of beauty.

O dear one, let there not be a breaking of your waist—which is bent down by the weight of your uplifted lotus-bud breasts and heavy sighs, and which is graced by the waves of the three folds—nor let it be shattered.
(Offstage: Ho there, attendants! Where is Rāma, the son of Daśaratha?
Women: Alas! It is he himself who calls out.
Rāma: This roar of his voice—deep as the thundering of the Puṣkara and Āvartaka clouds—belonging to one whose deeds are fierce with tireless audacity, fills my ear-cavities with delight.
(Thus she walks about.
Sītā: What is the point? (Holding her bow: Noble husband, we must not go while our father has not yet returned.
Friends! My dear friend's modesty has now been overturned by a change of emotion.
Rāma: (To himself) I am conquered by affection. (Aloud) In that case, I shall set aside my bow and depart.
(Offstage:
"O, sirs! O, sirs! The water has spilled! and so forth; he recites it again.)
Sītā: Then I shall hold it by force.
Rāma: Alas!
On one hand, my arrival before this overflowing treasury of ascetic power and prowess draws me toward it through my love for the company of the virtuous and my impetuous passion for heroism;
on the other hand, this embrace of Vaidehī—cool as yellow sandalwood and the moon, tender and blissful, yet causing my consciousness to repeatedly fade away—holds me back. (22)

Friends! Here he comes—indeed, that great Rākṣasa of all the Kṣatriyas. He has arrived, wielding a flaming axe whose luster makes his body appear radiant as it is gazed upon by the light of the blazing sun; the mass of his matted hair is indistinguishable from the thousands of flames of a forest fire tossing about in disarray; and the earth is rendered helpless by the crushing impact of his broad, pillar-like thighs, which are cast out with wide strides.

Rāma: This is that descendant of Bhṛgu, the sole hero of the three worlds, the sage who is like a vast, unassailable mass of splendors; he is as if the very union of majesty and ascetic power incarnate, a heroic essence that has taken on a solid form, as fierce as it is radiant. (23)

(With wonder) Though his deeds are terrible, he is a storehouse of meritorious vows; possessing immeasurable power, he shines like the Atharvan Veda itself, assuming a form that is both beautiful and fearsome. 24.

For this is the fierce essence of power of the God of gods, the conqueror of Tripura, who, when enraged, assumes the nature of the fire of Kālarudra to bring about the destruction of the eons; appearing now under the guise of Brahmā, he has risen up as if a single mass, yet distinct, capable of churning the entire multitude of worlds. (25)
(Smiling) Oh, how wonderful is the diversity of the venerable one’s independent will!
A battle-axe, matted with a mass of blazing flames, rests upon his shoulder; upon his body are matted locks, a bow, bark garments, and a deerskin.
An arrow flashes in his hand, encircled by a moving rosary of rudrākṣa beads; thus his attire spreads a beauty that is a fusion of the fierce and the tranquil. (26)
"My dear, this man is a guru; therefore, move away and veil yourself."
Sītā: Alas, alas! He has already arrived! (Folding her hands in supplication) Noble Lord, save me! My beloved impetuous one, be gracious!
Rāma: O beloved! This is a sage, and moreover a hero such as he; that is pleasing to me. Cease this trembling, O timid one; you are a Kṣatriya woman.
In this world, I am the descendant of Raghu, a Kṣatriya whose fame is spread abroad and whose arms itch with the pride of battle. (27)
(Then enters the enraged Paraśurāma. Paraśurāma: Oh, what a lack of self-knowledge on the part of that wicked Kṣatriya youth!

He was not terrified even when the bow of the Lord, the husband of Bhavānī, was shattered by him—a bow belonging to the Blessed One whose soul is pacified by a continuous stream of compassion for all living beings.
But his son Skanda—by whom the world was made to celebrate the slaying of Tāraka blinded by intoxication—is dear like Skanda himself; or else, how have I, his disciple, been forgotten? (28)
This is the harsh consequence of my tranquility:
that sovereignty has once again been established even among the Kṣatriyas, and by them alone have bows been taken up once more;
and by me too, who was intoxicated by the strength of my arms, have unrestrained deeds been heard of once again. (29)
Rāma:

While the sage—whose greatness of ascetic power, splendor, and heroism is immeasurable, who is a treasury of fame, and who is inflated with unfounded pride—rushes toward me in rage, my hand throbs impetuously both for the act of displaying mastery in the new science of archery and for clasping his feet. (30)
However, it is not, for now, the object of conventional practice.
Jāmadagnya: Ho there, attendants! Where is Rāma, the son of Daśaratha?
Rāma: Here I am, sir; this way, this way, please.
Jāmadagnya: Well done, Prince! Well done! You are indeed truly an Ikṣvāku.

Though I am searching for you to destroy you, you, whose being is pure by birth, offer yourself up out of pride—just as a young cub of a lordly scent-elephant offers itself to the lion, the lord of beasts, whose thunderbolt-like claws crush the peaks of the frontal globes of elephants.
Women [are] the purifiers of existing, obstructed inauspiciousness.
Jāmadagnya:
(Gazing; to himself) What a charming young kṣatriya he was!
This child, bearing a form adorned with five flickering locks of hair—both innocent yet bold, profound and captivating, marked by the signs of innate splendor.
Even though he is merely a deer, he captivates my mind at once with the splendor of his quintessential beauty; yet he must be slain—alas, fie upon the cruelty of a hero’s vow! //32//
(Aloud:

May this flaming axe, hurled in an instant by the pillar-like arm of the formidable Bhārgava—impelled by the wrath arising from the splitting asunder of Śiva’s bow, which had never before been bent by Niśumbha—become a guest upon the surface of your neck, so that by this very act the Lord Hara may be proclaimed throughout the worlds as Khaṇḍaparaśu (“He whose Axe is Broken”). (33)
Women: Alas, alas! This one is truly ablaze!
Rāma:

(Gazing with composure, great respect, and curiosity) This is that very axe which was indeed bestowed as a favor upon you by the blessed Nīlalohita, when he was pleased by your victory over Kārttikeya and his retinue, and which you have held for a thousand years as your pupil.

Friends: Princess, look! With his heart overflowing with respect, yet restrained by his unshakable fortitude and firmness, the noble prince laughs at the attainment of the divine Bhagīratha’s purpose. Sītā looks on with wonder and tears.
Jāmadagnya:

(To himself) A marvel, a marvel! This is indeed a different kind of person altogether. Such is this greatness and benevolence, whose basis is entirely beyond comprehension; and such is the display of manly prowess, profound and steady despite its intensity.
(Aloud) Ah, O son of Daśaratha, this is that very axe, dear to the feet of my preceptor.
Friends! It is as if we have been conversing while sitting for a long time.
Jāmadagnya:
Even in the tumultuous contest of practicing with weapons, though surrounded by the hosts of the Gaṇas' armies, the prince was indeed conquered by me.
Yet, embracing me and showing his favor even for this much, my venerable preceptor, who is fond of virtue, bestowed this [weapon] upon me. (34)
Rāma: (To himself) How is it that he speaks even with so much [arrogance]? Oh, what an expansion of pride and self-importance!
(Aloud: Therefore, O Blessed One, your reputation as a hero has spread throughout heaven and earth.
It is by that very [reputation] that the Blessed Lord Khaṇḍaparaśu, the fierce husband of Caṇḍī and preceptor of the three worlds, has become renowned;
and it is by that same [reputation], earned through the victory over the enemy of the stars (Rāvaṇa), that your fame has attained its splendor as Paraśurāma. (35)
Furthermore:

His birth was from Jamadagni; that Blessed Lord is the wielder of the Pināka bow and the preceptor of the gods. As for his prowess, it is surely not within the path of words, for it is made manifest by his deeds.

His renunciation reached its limit in the selfless gift of the entire earth sealed by the seven oceans—what, indeed, is not extraordinary about that Blessed One, who is a treasure-house of truth, sacred knowledge, and austerity? (36)
Friends, noble ladies, you know how very delightful it is to converse.
Jāmadagnya:

O Rāma, O Rāma! Bearing a loveliness of countenance that is worthy of your inner disposition, you—possessing a beauty of virtues beyond all conjecture—are in every way truly captivating to my heart. (37)
Moreover:

My chest, scarred by the wounds of Viśākha’s arrows and its single side bruised by the pestle-like tusk of Heramba, stands bristling with horripilation from the attainment of this wondrous heroism; truly I say, it seems to desire to embrace you. (38)
Friends! Noble daughter, look at the good fortune of the noble lord! You, indeed, being constantly averse to him, are deceiving yourself.
(Sītā, weeping, regains her composure.)
Rāma: Venerable sir, this [request for] an embrace is contrary to what was intended.
Friends, his modesty is adorned by his own steadfastness and gentleness.
Jāmadagnya:

(To himself) Oh, how the heart of this prince is purified by a nobility that embraces the excellence of another's virtues! Yet, there is a great egoism here—difficult to perceive due to his ultimate humility—and graspable only by a most subtle intellect.
Even as I am captivated by the exceedingly wonderful states of this extraordinary character, I nevertheless feel a sense of detachment.
This is some being in the form of a heroic child, consisting of a collection of the essence of immeasurable greatness. //39//
How wonderful!
It is conceivable that his body here radiates the mass of merit from the gift of fearlessness to the world;
for it shines with prosperity, with splendor ignited by virtuous qualities, and with righteousness, human victory, and valor. (40)

For he is indeed like the science of weaponry incarnate, having manifested in bodily form as if to protect the worlds; like the duty of the warrior class (*kṣatra-dharma*) taking on a physical body for the sake of guarding the treasury of the Veda; like a collection or an accumulation of all powers and virtues; and like a mass of the world’s merit manifesting and remaining present. (41)
(Aloud: Ladies, let this bride enter the inner apartments.
Rāma: (To himself) It is exactly so.
(Offstage:
Siradhvaja, bow in hand, is approaching from this very direction, accompanied by Gautama Śatānanda, the family priest of the Janakas. (42)
Friends, my lady, our father has already arrived; come, let us enter within.
Sītā:
(To herself) O Goddess Saṅgrāmaśrī, here is my salutation with joined palms to you.
(Thus the women exit. Jāmadagnya:
This is King Janaka, the wise one, protected by his family priest, the descendant of Aṅgiras.
It is said that Yājñavalkya was a disciple of Āditya, to whom the Sage revealed the supreme Brahman. //43//
He is of virtuous conduct; nevertheless, the fact that he is a kṣatriya causes me a throbbing pain in my head.
(Then enter Janaka and Śatānanda, both in a state of agitation.
Śatānanda: O King, what is appropriate here?
Janaka: O Blessed One, if this sage is a guest, let water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and thereafter the honey-mixture (madhuparka) be prepared for this Vedic scholar.
But if he is an enemy, a sudden hater of my son and treasure, then here, in the absence of policy, the bow has its authority. (44)
Thus they walk about.
Rāma: Why then has the venerable one shed tears?
Jāmadagnya: Nothing at all.
When pleasures arise together in the mind, they spread a supreme abundance; there, when it has entered the path of vision, a festival for the eyes initiates delight.

Yet you, though still fresh as a bridegroom wearing the wedding bracelet, glorious and dear to the heart—you must be slain! Alas, because you have insulted your guru, we are already pained by this very thought.
Rāma: Bhārgava, it is understood that you feel compassion for me.

Jāmadagnya: Oh, have you been saved after all? How could an axe fall upon the throat of one like you—whose neck is as smooth as a conch shell, and whose firm frame is as glossy as a cloud filled with nectar? (46)
Rāma: It is indeed true that you have been rejected out of compassion.
Jāmadagnya: Ah! He has turned his frown upon me alone! O wretched Kṣatriya child, that you—though a mere infant—should take a young bride for yourself; this causes us unprecedented distress.
This is a well-known proverb, sung as a traditional saying:
"Rāma Jāmadagnya himself severed the head of his own mother. (47)
Moreover, you fool!

Having repeatedly torn out and hacked to pieces even fetuses out of rage for the Kṣatriya lineage, and having exterminated all royal dynasties on every side up to twenty-one times, my true nature is surely known to all beings—that I am now making the fire of my wrath subside through the great joy of a sacrifice in a lake filled with their blood, which was inherited from my father. (48)
Rāma: Indeed, cruelty is a fault of the person in such a case; what need is there for boasting about it?
Jāmadagnya: O Kṣatriya youth! You are indeed becoming too arrogant. Strike!
Let the bow bend; for I am one who delights in the first blow. But once I have struck you down, what can another do?
With the bond of his hard shoulders severed by the axe—resplendent like a belched-up flame from a spreading fire—the headless trunk (kabandha) suddenly bursts forth. 49.
Janaka and Śatānanda: Dear Rāmabhadra, remain here for now with full confidence.
Rāma: Why have I become one who requires permission?
Jāmadagnya: Is it well with you, O descendant of Aṅgiras?
Śatānanda: Especially because of the sight of you. Moreover, you are our most venerable guest, provided that we are capable of offering hospitality.

Jāmadagnya: O priest, he is one of virtuous conduct, a master of the Vedas (*śrotriya*), a householder, and a disciple of Yājñavalkya; in his case, everything is appropriate. However, I have no desire for hospitality.

Śatānanda: Our established custom has been violated by you entering the maiden’s inner apartments without permission. Jāmadagnya: I am a forest-dwelling Brahmin, unacquainted with the domestic customs of the supreme lord’s household.
Rāma: It is indeed fitting that one who has bestowed the entire world as a sacrificial fee should display such an outburst of pride toward his vassal kings.
Janaka: How can you desire a sinful deed against the child of the Raghus, while we stand as his protectors? (Entering) Chamberlain:
O King, the queens have assembled for the loosening of the marriage bracelets; let an attendant be sent. (50)
Janaka and Śatānanda:
Dear Rāmabhadra, your mother-in-law calls for you; therefore, please go. Rāma: Venerable son of Jamadagni, so the gurus command.

Jāmadagnya: What is the harm? Let the worldly custom be observed; let your kinsmen see you. However, forest-dwellers do not remain for long in the haunts of men. I am desirous of departing; therefore, time must not be wasted.
Rāma: So be it.
(Entering) Sumantra: The venerable Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra summon you, along with Bhārgava.
The others: Where are the two venerable ones?
Sumantra: In the presence of the great king Daśaratha.
Rāma: We shall go according to the word of our preceptor.
(Thus they all exit.
//The Second Act//
Oṃ āḥ praḥ svāhā.
